cards.explanation: The answer is a farmer, friends. James says, "See how the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the soil…" A farmer plants the seed and then has to wait, and he can't make a single sprout come up faster. I've stood over dough begging it to rise, so I know that feeling.

The answer is rains, friends. James says the farmer is patient for the fall and spring rains. Those are the rains his crop is waiting on. No rain, no harvest, and the farmer can't order it like a delivery.

The answer is False. James says, "You, too, be patient and strengthen your hearts, because the Lord’s coming is near." So the patience he asks for comes with a reminder that the Lord's coming is near. I don't know the day, and James doesn't give one either.

The answer is True, friends. James says, "Do not complain about one another, brothers, so that you will not be judged." Waiting can make people grumpy, and the grumbling lands on whoever is standing closest. James tells the brothers not to do it.

The answer is Judge, friends. James says, "Look, the Judge is standing at the door!" He says it right after telling the brothers not to complain about one another. It's a serious line, and Judge is the word James picks.

The answer is the prophets who spoke in the Lord's name, friends. James says, "…take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord." He calls them an example of patience in affliction. They spoke for the Lord, and James holds them up so the brothers can see what patient endurance looks like.

The answer is Job, friends. James says, "You have heard of Job’s perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord." He puts the perseverance and the outcome side by side. I think that's the kind of story you tell someone who's tired of waiting, and James says the outcome came from the Lord.

The answer is that the Lord is full of compassion and mercy, friends. James says, "The Lord is full of compassion and mercy." He says it right after pointing to Job's outcome from the Lord. Patient waiting isn't aimed at someone cold, and James wants the brothers to know that.

The answer is swear, friends. James says, "Above all, my brothers, do not swear, not by heaven or earth or by any other oath." He says "above all," so this one matters to him. The way he finishes the verse says a plain yes and no are all they need.
The answer is False. James says, "Simply let your “Yes” be yes, and your “No,” no…" So a plain yes or no is enough. If I say yes, I'd better mean yes, and the words don't need any extra decoration.

The answer is sing praises, friends. James says, "Is anyone cheerful? He should sing praises." So the suffering person prays, and the cheerful person sings. I'd say pull out the loud voice for this one, because a happy heart has somewhere to send all that joy.

The answer is the elders of the church, friends. James says, "He should call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord." The sick person calls them, and they come to pray. Nobody has to sit alone with it.

The answer is True, friends. James says the elders should "…pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord." The sick person is the one who calls them. The prayer and the oil are both right there, and the verse ends with "…in the name of the Lord."

The answer is restore, friends. James says, "…the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick." He follows it with, "The Lord will raise him up." It's all about the Lord doing the lifting, and nobody else gets the credit.

The answer is that he will be forgiven, friends. James says, "If he has sinned, he will be forgiven." It comes right after the Lord raises up the sick one. I like that the promise sits right next to the prayer.

The answer is False. James says, "The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail." It isn't only prophets who pray with great power. He backs it up in the very next verse with Elijah, a prophet (1 Kings 18:36) whom he calls a man just like us (James 5:17).

The answer is that it would not rain, friends. James says Elijah "…prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain on the land for three and a half years." That's a big prayer from a man James calls just like us. Elijah was a prophet in Israel (1 Kings 18:36).
The answer is years, friends. James says it did not rain on the land for three and a half years. That's a long time to wait on the weather. And it all started with one man's earnest prayer.

The answer is crops, friends. James says, "Again he prayed, and the heavens gave rain, and the earth yielded its crops." After all that dry time, the rain came and the ground gave its crops. Elijah prayed, and the heavens answered.

The answer is that he will save his soul from death, friends. James says, "Whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover over a multitude of sins." Bringing a wandering brother back matters a great deal to him. He puts real weight on it.
